While the Government made a commitment to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts in respect of income tax remissions, I am tabling these tariff remission orders in the spirit of openness and transparency and because of the similarity between the two types of remissions.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from a number of constituents who point out that the Conservative Government does not have a mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States.
They believe that the trade agreement negotiated by the federal Government threatens the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership and to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadians or to equalize the opportunities between the regions of the country.
They also point out that the proposed deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future which thereby undermines our ability as a country to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
Since this denies Canadians the secure access to the U.S. market that was the key objective in these trade negotiations
from the outset, and since it also threatens the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs, they are asking Parliament now to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement in a general election.

speechtext:

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to speak to this legislation. Our caucus has taken the position that we support the legislation, although we have many concerns with it and with the Government's action in this particular area. It is not a new concern. This is something that we have been concerned about not only with this Government but also with the previous Government.
I know you were not a Member of Parliament, Madam Speaker, when the Liberals formed the Government in the years between 1980 and 1984, but you will recall that in those years the Liberals talked about a western development fund of some $4 billion. A certain percentage of that money was supposed to go to the native people in western Canada. That became a phantom fund. It was promised and repromised. Certainly Ministers of the Liberal Government, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), and others went to western Canada and talked about how valuable that fund would be for developing western Canada, and how important that fund would be for the native people of western Canada. Yet that money was never received.
That is one of the concerns that we have when we look at this legislation. I know that we are not alone. This legislation which is centred in Atlantic Canada has created many questions for people in that region. They are wondering if there will be new money, or is it merely the situation, which we believe to be true, that this is money that has already been taken from the region as a result of cut-backs and other programs. We are in a situation now where some of that money is being promised back to Atlantic Canada as if it was new money. That is an unfortunate situation. Of all the regions in this country that need more funding and deserve more funding, there is not one that deserves and needs it more than Atlantic Canada.
January 26, 1988

As a Member of the New Democratic Party caucus I have travelled throughout Atlantic Canada and gone through all the provinces there. I have gone to Labrador. I recognize how great that need is. It is disappointing to see a Government which has actually taken money from regional development over the last three and a half years now promising that it will do something new.
As I stated, we support the legislation because we recognize the need to do something in Atlantic Canada. But we have some legitimate concerns. I am sure when this legislation gets to committee, which I suspect it will do either some time today or tomorrow, through our caucus spokesperson, the Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris), we will have an opportunity to explain what type of changes must be made to this legislation.
We believe that the only way any region of this country can be developed, whether it is the west, or a northern riding like mine in Churchill, Manitoba, or whether it is Atlantic Canada, is by having the people in the region make the final decisions. If we are in a situation, which this legislation allows for yet again, where recommendations come from the region but the decisions are made on a political basis in Ottawa whenever the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) can spare the time to go to Atlantic Canada and make an announcement, then we are not achieving anything new. That is the problem. [DOT]
I understand that Mr. Rino Volpe, who is a member of the Atlantic Advisory Committee, told a class of business students at the University of Moncton just yesterday that he is frustrated by the set-up of the agency because it does not adequately take business interests into consideration. He is already considering resigning from the board. He shares the concerns expressed earlier by the President of the Atlantic Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Rick DesBrisay, who called the Atlantic Advisory Committee a toothless tiger.
Here we are with a member of the advisory committee already considering resignation and with the President of the Atlantic Chamber of Commerce calling the committee a toothless tiger. Why are they saying these things? It is because they believe that it has no decision-making power.
It is interesting to note that Mr. Volpe was also speaking as the President of the Conseil Economique du Nouveau Brunswick. He was not only expressing his individual concerns but the concerns of the group which he represents. Also in his speech yesterday he explained that the advisory committee would have no say over the selection of public servants in the agency. His primary concern is that decisions will not be made in the region.
I have gone through this kind of system before. The Government is just setting up a new form of regional decision making. Since 1977, before I was a Member of Parliament, in one form or another we have had a northern development agreement in
Government Organization Act. Atlantic Canada, 1987
my riding. We have had an agency in the North of federal government people working with provincial government people, and we have an advisory committee which reports to a federal Minister and to a provincial Minister. The concept is good, that we would have representation from the native people and from the various groups which composed northern Manitoba. They are an advisory council, just like this piece of legislation calls for. However, the problem is that in the regulations and in the way it is set up, all they do is give advice. They do not make decisions. Therefore we in northern Manitoba are in the situation which Mr. Volpe and Mr. DesBrisay have already expressed concern about. They are concerned that they will be in the same position, that decisions will not be made in the region, and that decisions will be made for political purposes. I know how badly that works.
As the Hon. Member for St. John's East expressed so eloquently in the House, if one is to sit on the committee and work with the people making representations, and if one has some understanding of the people of Moncton, of Saint John, of St. John's, of Charlottetown, or of any other community whether it be Halifax or Cape Breton, one must realize that the business people who will be making presentations have talked with the local mayor and council and with the local labour council. They understand what is needed and what can work in the region. Surely to God we should be in a situation where the people who serve on these advisory committees have the ability to make decisions.
1 recognize that the final dollars are federal dollars and that the federal Government and Cabinet should have ultimate control as they have ultimate responsibility for what is happening in any of their programs. However, that does not mean that we cannot have decision making taking place in the regions. The regions of the country are developed by co-operative community development.
1 can understand the federal Government, through its Ministers and the cabinet decision-making process, wanting and needing the right to say yes or no. However, it should not be saying yes or no to each and every project. It should be saying yes or no to the framework of the legislation, what kinds of programs are acceptable, and what kind of guidelines are necessary. That should be the function of the Government, and that is all the Government should be responsible for. 1 believe that the Government is responsible for its programs and that it should be in a position of setting the guidelines. I know that you realize, Madam Speaker, that the people in your region are capable of making decisions which are necessary for the region. It does not make sense to me that we should set up a structure where we bring in very talented people who know their regions only let them give advice. I support Mr. Volpe and Mr. DesBrisay when they say that it is a toothless tiger. Unfortunately this is happening yet again.

January 26, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
As I said earlier, since 1977 we in northern Manitoba have had a very similar program. We have gone through the growing pains. At present we have had an extension of our third agreement. We know that we will be renegotiating a new agreement over the next two years, and we know how necessary it is to take the decision-making process from Ottawa and put it within the province or, even better, within the region involved. Obviously, with regard to Atlantic Canada, that is the situation which needs to be developed.
1 am afraid that we will be in the situation which I expressed earlier of having decisions made on a political basis only. I am afraid that, because there is pressure at a certain time, the money will be used to help Cape Breton one year or Moncton the next year, and that all sorts of announcements will be made just prior to the upcoming election on the basis of the best information available, not on the basis of information that would be there had the power to make decisions been given to the people of Atlantic Canada.
One problem which all of us face as Members of Parliament is that decisions are not made in the House of Commons. Decisions are often made not only by senior federal government employees but quite often by federal government employees. The reason for this is that we pass legislation such as the measure before us. We are setting up an advisory committee which can give advice. We have a federal Government which is dissatisfied with its situation in the political polls at this time and is obviously very concerned about its ability to be re-elected. Real decision making is not made by Members of Parliament or by people in the regions. They end up being made by people working in the departments.
1 have no problem with federal government employees giving advice on which programs are good, which programs are not good, what kind of changes should be made to programs, or whether there should be training components in programs. All these things make sense, and we are hiring people to give us good advice. However, the problem is that federal government employees are working within their own regime. They are not necessarily emotionally involved in the development of a region. They are very often concerned about what they believe their Minister may or may not want. They are also concerned about what are their opportunities for advancement. [DOT]
[DOT] (M30)
I have seen the situation within my own riding. 1 am sure people from Atlantic Canada, the Member for St. John's East, for instance, can give other examples of people making decisions which might make sense in Toronto, Ottawa or Winnipeg but do not make sense in the regions which they actually affect. We are often in a situation where programs do not make sense for a region. I can give all sorts of examples.
Let me talk about Canada Mortgage and Housing. We have the same rules with regard to the percentage of income that
must be given to the Government if people are in federal government sponsored housing-it may be a provincial government program as well-whether they live in Toronto or northern Manitoba. I will explain that a little further. The federal Government requires that if you are living in a subsidized house, a house the Government has helped build, 25 per cent of one's gross income must be used to pay the mortgage. This makes sense in some areas where there is competition and other housing people can go into. But what if you make a large income and you are paying 25 per cent of it to live in a house, but your income goes up and up and up. All of a sudden you do not want to pay 25 per cent of your income to live in a CMHC sponsored house? What if you decide to move elsewhere?
This is a lovely principle, and it makes sense to some degree in the Torontos, Montreals and Ottawas of this world. But when you get into a northern community, whether northern Saskatchewan, as my friend from Prince Albert would talk about, northern Quebec or in some of the remote areas of Atlantic Canada, and the only housing available is federal Government sponsored housing where there is no land available, or serviced lots available, what then? You are stuck with this rule that makes sense in Toronto and Ottawa where options are available for people to move out.
In my riding there are houses with no water, no sewers, no municipal services. Because of the 25 per cent rule people are paying more for what could basically be called a cardboard shack. They are paying $500, $600 or $700 a month for a house without water, without sewers, without any of the services that we take for granted, a house which may have only 15-amp power. We say «You can build your own house.* But there are no lots available. You can have your own water and sewer but that is impossible because of the nature of the land.
The federal Government's rule-I do not want to pick on the Conservatives although they deserve all the picking on they can get-is a rule the Liberals brought in and it is the rule which the Tories have not yet had the political courage to change. The rule is that one pays 25 per cent of one's gross income for a federal government sponsored house regardless of where one lives in this country and regardless of whether there are other options available.
I was at a housing conference in northern Manitoba just a week and a half ago. People complained up and down about the problems. They complained that they cannot build log houses under the federal government program. They complained about the houses which might look nice in a southern suburb, a suburb of Toronto, a suburb of Calgary or any of the other communities I have mentioned earlier, but which make absolutely no sense in the communities in which they are being built. CMHC is a national program. The rules make sense in some parts of the country but they do not make sense right across the nation.
January 26, 1988

We are again setting up a new agency. We have very talented people in the Atlantic region who are willing to serve on the advisory committee and who understand how development should take place in their own regions. But we are denying them the real decision-making power. Why are Conservatives, who in 1979 talked about a community of communities, doing exactly as the previous Government did? Why are the Conservatives following exactly the same structures as the federal Liberals did in the programs which they developed for northern Manitoba?
I can go back to my speeches of 1979, 1980, 1981, 1982 and 1983 and feel like I am making almost the same speech again.
I really wonder if there was an election in 1984. It is so typical, Madam Speaker. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) makes his big promise during his Atlantic swing. When we finally get the details and we look at them-thanks to our new Member for St. John's East who has given us very good advice-I do not see any differences whatever from what the Liberals did in my riding through the Northern Development Agreement during the middle part of the 1970s and the early part of the 1980s.
I remember a Liberal Cabinet Minister, Pierre De Bane, who is now in the Senate, saying that the Liberals needed more political credit for what they were doing in northern Manitoba. Therefore they set up an office and a program. I looked at what he did and I look at what the Government is doing now and it is exactly the same.
I hope when this legislation gets to committee-we support the concept and principle of money going into Atlantic Canada because it is so necessary-that the Government and government Members who will be serving on that committee will allow the amendments necessary to make sure that the decisions are made in Atlantic Canada, that the community and co-operative development which the people in that region want can proceed and we do not have yet another political exercise.

Madam Speaker, would the Hon. Member elaborate on some of the very fine points he has made so that the Government could have the benefit of his experience and insight into these matters?
The Member touched on the very important matter of political patronage being a major feature of this type of development where a board or political appointee winds up advising the Minister to do the patronage thing. He talked about the problem of having new money available for these programs. Often the Government announces spending that is already in place basically in an attempt to deceive people. The Member from Churchill (Mr. Murphy) mentioned that this program has little support from the Atlantic Chamber of Commerce and a number of others.
Will the Member develop these points so the Government could have the benefit of his knowledge and experience of the Manitoba situation?
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly). He always asks some good questions. Unfortunately he never tells his caucus Whip what questions he is going to ask before he does so. Obviously this is not the situation of a planted question and a planted answer. Let me express some of my concerns.
There is an estimation that in Atlantic Canada as a result of the federal government cut-backs over $1.5 billion annually has been cut from various federal government programs going into Atlantic Canada. The amount of money here, although as usual the federal government likes to talk about $1 billion for this program and a billion for that program, is a billion dollars over five years. I have quoted the Chamber of Commerce and others. I have not been quoting those groups that are normally considered to be New Democratic supporters. The Government has taken away $1.5 billion from the various programs that used to benefit Atlantic Canada and has replaced that with a program which will give Atlantic Canadians at best $200 million a year. The net effect is that money is being lost.
I see that the Minister in charge of the western diversification office has entered the House. He understands that the same thing applies in western Canada. He now has a grand political machine and he is in a position of making decisions, but the people in the west know that they have suffered as a result of government cut-backs. They also object to the fact that the decision making will be done in Ottawa.
That is not just my perception or the perception of the Chamber of Commerce. According to The Globe and Mail of June 27, 1987, Senator Lowell Murray, the Minister in charge of this agency, said that the final decisions will be made by him in Ottawa. Those were his words.
I do not understand why there is a political need to have all decisions made in Ottawa. It seems to me that since the Government appoints the advisory board, it already has control through its ability to say who will be on the board and what groups will be represented. That advisory board is accountable to a Minister. The Government already has control.
I also recognize that the Government is in a position to set regulations and pass legislation. It has the ultimate control over the purse, as it should. Why not let people in the regions make the decisions? That is what we are asking for and that is what we believe is so fundamental to the entire process.
Makes sense.
The Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), a Member from the community of Toronto which I have been attacking for the last little while, has said that it makes sense.

January 26, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
If the Government wants real political credit in Atlantic Canada, western Canada or the North-
How about the Pacific coast?

Even the Pacific coast. The Hon. Member is from the Pacific coast and his riding spans the waters. The Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River understands what I am trying to say.
If the Government wants political credit, then it should make the change. It should not be like the Liberals. It should not be afraid to let the people in the regions make decisions. It should not want political credit for every grant that is given, and grants are not given unless a cabinet Minister is travelling through the area or the Prime Minister attends an opening of winter games or something of that nature. The Government should trust the people in Atlantic Canada, western Canada and even the City of Toronto to make the decisions which make sense for the regions.
I challenge the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. McKnight), who is also in charge of the western diversification office, to let that happen. Do not make sure that the Prime Minister is travelling through western Canada before making promises. As we know, the Prime Minister has actually stopped in Manitoba twice since 1984. We believe he came in the middle of the night because he has not had the courage to come to Manitoba in the daytime.
The people in the regions know their regions and they know what programs will work. If they make the decision, we will not get stuck with a bunch of political patronage and opportunism, all those things which create so much havoc in the House of Commons. We are saying to the Government that it should let the people who know the regions make the decisions.

Madam Speaker, I am actually very glad the Hon. Member brought this up. Without telling secrets about our caucus executive meeting this morning, I can say that this issue was discussed. I will not go into the details of it, but the gist of the decision that was made-

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Why not?

The Minister who is in charge of the western diversification office, who is also the Minister of Indian Affairs when he has the time, has asked why not. If he is willing to tell us what happens in Cabinet, I am willing to tell him what happens in caucus, but I do not think that that was the gist of the question.
We are very concerned with how decisions are made. People like me who are from Manitoba are very concerned about the way the decision on the CF-18 was made. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) said in the House that it would cost only S3.5 million or $4 million more to build in Quebec, and on technical advice he said that both groups were pretty well equal. As we know, the information that came out over Christmas as a result of the access to information law indicated that it cost a heck of a lot more for the contract to go to Quebec. One estimate was that it cost $65 million more, but that was denied by the Conservatives. The Chairman of the Conservative caucus, the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay), said that it did not cost $65 million more for the contract to go to Quebec, it cost a lot less. He said that he actually knew the information but no one had ever asked him. Someone finally got around to asking him. He said that it would only cost $26 million more for the contract to go to Quebec.
We have said in the House and will say to members of our caucus when they step out of line that these decisions should not be made on a political basis. They should be done after an open and honest tendering system, regardless of where you live. Whether it is Saint John, and I have toured the dry docks there and I know they are very good facilities, or Montreal or Winnipeg, you have to know that you are playing on, to use an expression of the Prime Minister, a level playing field. You must know what is going on. Not like the poor people of Manitoba who bid on a contract they did not have a hope in hell of getting. Let us make the system fair, that is what we are saying.
January 26, 1988

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I must interrupt the Hon. Member because the time for questions and comments has now expired.
As we are resuming debate, I must advise the House that from now on, according to our rules, the speeches will be subject to a 10-minute limitation.

Madam Speaker, 10 minutes is certainly enough time in which to talk about this Bill, I can tell you that. After reading the Bill and after looking at some of the promises made by the Government in introducing it, one would have to come to the conclusion that it is perhaps not even worth 10 minutes. The organization itself is nothing more than a political structure or political announcement to try and give the people of Atlantic Canada the impression that the Government is really interested in the problems of Atlantic Canada. That is all it is.
As the Bill itself says, all it will do is co-ordinate matters related to the federal Government in Atlantic Canada. In other words, all of the announcements being made regarding this agency are being made with funding which is already in place through an existing agency such as DR1E which we all know about. This $1.05 billion is really nothing to shout about at all.
A good indication of the importance of this agency is that the person in charge of the agency, the most senior person, the ultimate boss, should have been a cabinet Minister but is not. Perhaps we have lost sight of that. He is not even a cabinet Minister in the House of Commons. This glorious new Bill is not sponsored in the House of Commons by a cabinet Minister. The person responsible is a Senator.
The Senator the Government chose to head the agency-the Minister said he is the Hon. Member for-

speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: He is a member of the Cabinet of the Parliament of Canada.

The only real attribute of the Senator that I can see is that he is from New Waterford, Nova Scotia.
I believe you have to direct your questions in the House about this agency to the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). He is answerable in the House on behalf of Senator Murray who has been put in charge of this Bill. That is an indication of how important this agency is to the Government of Canada.
If you look at the opinions expressed by some reputable people in Atlantic Canada on the CBC radio this morning, they quote a Mr. Volpe, President of the Economic Council of New Brunswick, past President of the New Brunswick branch of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, Vice-President of the Chamber of Commerce of Edmundston, and member of the Board of Directors for the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. He sits on the New Brunswick Forestry Products Commission as well. He is quoted this morning as saying that
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
the agency is not working. It is really not doing what the Government of Canada said it was going to do. It is really not originating the ideas from Atlantic Canada and funding those ideas. In other words, it is not working, according to Mr. Volpe.
I forgot to mention that Mr. Volpe is a government appointee to the board in charge of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. He is on the board appointed by the Government. When you have a member of the advisory board appointed by the Government saying the agency is not working, then obviously something is seriously wrong with the agency.
That is all there is to say about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. They should call it the Atlantic Canada overblown agency. All we have heard about it is rhetoric from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Ministers from Atlantic Canada, and there is nothing there. There is absolutely nothing at all in the Bill that is going to help Atlantic Canada. Not one single thing is there, not one thing. In every program that you see there has been a reduction in the amount of money going into Atlantic Canada.
If the Government of Canada is really interested in doing something for Atlantic Canada, it would address the inshore fishermen of Newfoundland who are up here today trying to get a meeting with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), trying to find out why the Government of Canada increased the quota of northern cod. In other words, it is robbing the industries around Newfoundland of fish. It is bowing down to the Government of France.
Yesterday or the day before when France announced that it was going to catch 26,000 tonnes of codfish, the Government just bent over backwards and said it can't do anything about this because it is the Government of France and the French are over here catching Canadian fish. Oh, we cannot send out a boat to try and arrest them. Oh, no. That is the Government of France. However, if that were a Nova Scotian or New Bruns-wicker or Prince Edward Islander or Newfoundlander or Quebecer, oh, yes, drag them into court and charge them.
The whole direction of the Government of Canada is off. It walks in here with this Bill and says the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, what we call the Atlantic Canada overblown agency, is the new future of Atlantic Canada. We are saying that the Government is fouling up everything else. The future is sitting out there right now. All it has to do is address the problems it has created.
I know my 10 minutes are about up and I thank the House for its indulgence. As I say, there is nothing to this Bill. It will go down in history as being a nothing Bill with 300 employees and no budget. The Government is underspending for this year, according to the Prime Minister, because the Government does not want to give the agency the authority to spend any money.

January 26, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987

Madam Speaker, I must commend the Eton. Member for that eloquent and hard-hitting speech. I think he really elucidated the shallowness of the present Government in its dealings with Atlantic Canadians.
Certainly the Bill before us today can only be described as disappointing. When the Elon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) spoke, he spent some time outlining the whole purpose of these kinds of things from the Government's point of view. It is a mechanism to try and obtain political credit.
It is interesting that one of the things which was not included in that discussion is that the Government has to do something significant before it can expect any political credit. Certainly the Bill before us today, proposing to set up an Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, is not doing anything constructive.
People in this House have spoken of the shortcomings, the fact that the board itself has no decision-making power, that Atlantic Canadians will not have an opportunity to determine which projects are appropriate for their region and which are not. In fact, many of those projects will be decided on the basis of political patronage. The Government has had a litany of patronage arrangements which have done irreparable harm to the Government. 1 cast my mind back to the tuna fish scam and the clam scam. Today we have what is being labelled as the lobster scam. Essentially it is more important for the Government to fill the pockets of its friends than to take care of the needs of Canadians. With some well-known pork-barrel-lers sitting on the board of this agency, political patronage once again looms its ugly head in the distribution of Government benefits. Therefore, it is an element of very serious concern raised by many people in this House.
There is talk of funding in the order of S200 million a year over a five-year period, something in the order of $1 billion. We have seen this operate in other areas before. In order to obtain political credit for doing nothing the Government simply reannounces existing spending programs or chops a program and then uses the funding for an equivalent kind of program under the guise of creating something new, of indicating an interest in the area and acknowledging its need, while only reshuffling existing dollars into the area. There is a great deal of concern that the new agency and the projects it recommends will not be receiving new dollars, that existing dollars which are allocated to meet certain needs in the region will be spent from a political patronage point of view.
Previous speakers mentioned that there is really no base of support for this organization, that it was created out of smoke and mirrors by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Organizations such as the Atlantic Canada Chamber of Commerce and various chambers of commerce in the region are criticizing it. There was no consultation in setting it up, there is no real decision-making power in the board and, as I said, there is no constituency for it. It has been termed a toothless tiger. The suggestion put forward by the Whip of the New Democratic Party
in his speech was that if the Government had any guts, any real demonstrated concern for Atlantic Canadians, the board would have the decision-making authority to determine projects which are relevant for the region.
The whole thrust of the Government in removing regional development programs is interesting. It brings to mind the difficulties that will be experienced under the Mulroney-Rea-gan trade deal. Under that trade arrangement with the United States opportunities for regional development subsidization to get certain industries in deprived or problem areas in the country operating will disappear. That arrangement will probably do serious harm, in many cases, to attempts to get industry going in Atlantic Canada under regional development.
There is a great deal of concern that where profitable opportunities do exist, rather than seeing them fall into the control of Canadians we may see American firms taking them over and operating them for, in many cases, benefits across the border. The Mulroney-Reagan trade arrangement will certainly be a major problem in this area.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-SUGGESTION UNITED STATES BE BILLED FOR DAMAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, only this Government is surprised by the unwillingness of the Americans to negotiate a treaty to stop acid rain coming across our border. The fact is that President Reagan only agreed to consider the possibility of a treaty, not to sign one. The U.S. State Department officials made this distinction clear on several occasions. Yet the Government tries to maintain the illusion of progress.

January 26, 1988
In 1985 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appointed an acid rain envoy to reinvent the wheel, in 1986 accepted the U.S. five-year research and demonstration program, and now discovers the true intent of the U.S. administration is not to cut transboundary air pollution, but to continue with research and development.
In 1985 the Government made the mistake of abandoning the multilateral, global policy approach to acid rain which served us well because it led to 21 nations signing the Helsinki Accord on Acid Rain.
We urge the Government to resume the global policy, and at the same time prepare a Bill to be presented to President Reagan at the next summit for compensation for damage caused each year to lakes, fisheries, agriculture, maple syrup producers, forestry, tourism, health, structures and buildings by acid rain pollution coming from the United States into Canada every day.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure today to recognize the thirty-eighth anniversary of India's Republic Day. In 1950 India became a republic. Like our Canada Day, India's Republic Day is its biggest national holiday.
Sharing similar aspirations of accommodating various ethnic and linguistic groups, India has tried to achieve a better democratic system and standard of living for its people. Canada, for its part, has made its contribution to India through various development efforts down through the years. In the international arena, Canada and India have shared values, particularly the desire to bring justice and peace to the world.
Canada has been made richer by having amongst its cultural mosiac Canadian citizens of Indian origin. I, for one, would vouch that they have made a tremendous contribution to our country and our Canadian society as a whole. I am proud to have citizens of all cultural origins in my riding of Etobicoke North, and today I am pleased to be able to pay a special tribute to those Canadians of Indian origin.

UNITED STATES-CALL FOR ENDING OF AID TO CONTRA FORCES

Mr. Speaker, today the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) leaves for a conference in Lusaka. Before he goes, once again I would like to urge upon him that the Canadian Government take a stronger position with respect to U.S. funding of the
Contras. In recent days we have seen that President Reagan has made this a priority for his political agenda. I would urge upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs that Canada finally come out and be explicitly critical of this particular preoccupation of President Reagan.
When I raised this matter in the House last week, the Secretary of State said that I was suggesting he attack the United States. I suggest no such thing. However, I do suggest that he be critical of the United States.
He states that it is not Canadian policy to offer advice to other Governments. We do offer advice to other Governments. In recent weeks we have offered advice to the Israeli Government. I see no reason why the United States of America should be exempt from criticism, and why we should make an exception when it comes to American foreign policy and feel that we cannot be critical of that particular country.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, I have often been critical in the House and in committees of the RCMP's role in terms of the promotion and advancement of female members of the force, and rightly so, but I am pleased today to give credit where credit is due in terms of a new initiative that the RCMP is taking to ensure equality for women within the force.
As I am sure Hon. Members know, the RCMP only started to hire women recruits in 1974, and it has been difficult for many of them to achieve the status of corporal. That has meant that of the 94 corporal level positions at the Training Academy in Regina there are no women. With the increasing number of women coming into the force, it is obvious that there is a need for women to be teaching in that instructional academy.

TAX REFORM -IMPORTANCE OF TAKING SITUATION OF SMALL GOLD-FIELDS INTO ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the crash, the small gold-fields are having a hard time, as can be seen in the article by Michel Girard published in the daily La Presse of January 25, 1988, under the title Periode difficile pour les auriferes juniors.
Despite an average drop of 40 per cent in the stock prices compared to before the stock exchange crisis and an increase in the price of gold, small gold-fields cannot seem to be able to take off again. And as we are sailing in a downward cycle, there is little chance of seeing small gold-fields come back in the medium-term to the peak they reached before the crash.
According to the mining analyst, David Charles, who is a researcher for the firm Tasse et Associes, investors would then
be well advised to bank on quality stock because of the difficult situation in the stock market.
On the other hand, we expect a seasonal recovery of small mining operations for February or March. Traditionally, there is such a recovery around that time, but nothing guarantees it will happen again this year. This period also coincides with the delivery of many flow-through shares bought in 1987.
I would like to bring this to the attention of the Finance Minister (Mr. Wilson) and of the Deputy Minister of Finance, Mr Stanley Hartt, so that they watch very closely that period and revise the tax reform accordingly.

POTATO EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES-NON-TARIFF BARRIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian potatoes are world renowned for their quality and taste. Too bad American inspectors don't agree.
When Maritime potatoes which have already been thoroughly inspected by Agriculture Canada cross the border into Maine, inspectors pick over them trying to find fault. Since the destination inspection is the final one, these first-line inspectors cannot stop the spuds from continuing on to New York, Boston, Philadelphia, and other eastern seaboard destinations.
However, they are harassing the industry by saying that they have to phone the end receiver and warn him of poor quality. Since many loads come through at night when receivers are not available, truck drivers must either wait or head back to Canada. There are some who persevere, however. Up to January 22, 20 out of 29 loads which were declared to be poor at the border passed reinspection at the end.
Maine is using this non-tariff barrier to keep New Brunswick potatoes out since its anti-dumping suit was not successful. The Government assured us that the trade agreement would prevent this type of action. It was wrong again.

TOBIAS HOUSE PROJECT IN TORONTO-LACK OF AFFORDABLE LAND

Mr. Speaker, Tobias House is a church-sponsored group with excellent experience in the case of disabled adults. subtopic: TOBACCO INDUSTRY-CALL FOR SUBSTANTIAL INCREASE IN TAXES
TOBACCO INDUSTRY-CALL FOR SUBSTANTIAL INCREASE IN TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the most difficult aspect of the legislation to ban tobacco advertising is the impact that it will have on funding for sports and cultural organizations.
Today the Cancer Society, along with other groups concerned with public health, proposed a solution. What these groups want is a substantial increase in tobacco taxes. Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment.
In view of the fact that a major reduction in acid rain emissions is essential to the survival of our waters and forests, especially in Quebec, what concrete strategy will the Government be using to convince the Americans of the need for specific reductions, especially in the midwest, within the shortest possible time frame? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member will know and the House will know as well, the Canadian Government has been seeking from the U.S. administration agreement on a proposal from our Government to slash American acid rain-causing emissions by 50 per cent by 1994 based on 1980 figures. That program would parallel exactly the program we have imposed on ourselves.
The Canadian negotiators went to Washington yesterday for a major meeting at which the American administration, through its negotiators, was to respond to our call. The initial response to our call for a bilateral accord was deeply disappointing. We are now discussing within the Cabinet, particularly among the Prime Minister, myself, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, our options and we will keep the House informed as the issue progresses.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister must know that the answer is more than deeply disappointing, it is a disaster for Canada.
Plan A was the envoy process. Plan B was the very meager promise written into the script of President Reagan's address here in Canada last year. Plan C was a propaganda program which was withdrawn because it was offending the wrong people. Does the Government have a Plan D now?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will be beginning on Monday of next week the first meeting of the Special Committee of the Commonwealth Foreign Ministers on South Africa. The agenda will involve a review of the areas set out for action by the Commonwealth Conference at Vancouver, including means by which we can look at ways of making sanctions that are in place more effective. Ways of encouraging greater dialogue between opponents of apartheid who live inside and outside South Africa will also be included. We will also be looking at ways in which we can encourage more productive dialogue within the region itself.
This is the first meeting in a process. It is designed not only to continue pressure upon the Government of South Africa to change the apartheid system but also to expand the capacities of those of us who are, as are all in this House, committed to an end to apartheid, to find ways in which real change might be encouraged.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise before the House today to move the adoption of the reply to the other place on Bill C-84. The Government proposes several amendments to the report before us.
Bill C-84 addresses an issue of grave concern to Canadians-the growing abuse of Canada's refugee claims process. The number of refugee claims received in Canada has grown from some 1,600 in 1980 to almost 30,000 in 1987. We have a backlog of more than 40,000 claims pending. The backlog is growing by 2,500 claims or more every month. Thousands of recent claimants have arrived with fraudulent documents or no documents at all. We cannot allow this situation to deteriorate even further.

January 26, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 are essential parts of this Government's strategy for restoring the integrity of Canada's immigration and refugee programs. The passage of Bill C-55 will establish a new refugee determination system in Canada.
Bill C-84 was introduced to send a message world-wide that Canada would no longer tolerate abuse and would deal with security risks.

I met with the Senate committee on December 8 at the conclusion of more than three months of hearings on the Bill. 1 informed the Senators that I would not change the principles or objectives of the Bill, but that I was willing to consider changes about which lawyers would have less to argue. I was also willing to consider any proposals that would clarify the Bill and further the achievement of our objectives.
Let me restate the objectives of Bill C-84. The primary objective of the Bill, as is stated in its preamble, is to protect genuine refugees. The Bill seeks to deter the wholesale abuse of the refugee claims system that has taken place over the last 10 years and to create a scheme of penalties to ensure that abusers are properly punished.
These provisions do not affect thousands of genuine refugees whom we bring to Canada each year. In short, they do not make it more difficult for people who need our help to obtain it.
Bill C-84 deals, however, with sanctions and penalties for persons who encourage illegal immigration to Canada and who knowingly abet the abuse of the refugee claims process. The Bill closes a loophole through which people who are criminals or terrorists can use the refugee claims system to defer their removal from Canada for many years.
The Bill also deals with detention for those who are security risks to the Canadian public, or those who conceal or destroy their identity documents so that we cannot easily discover who they are or from where they came.
We know that some 14,000 people have arrived in Canada with forged documents or no documents at all over the last two years. Most of these persons were not using forged documents in order to escape from the country in which they faced persecution, but rather to conceal the fact that they already had a safe haven somewhere else or that they had no real claim to refugee status at all.

This Bill, Madam Speaker, provides stiffer fines and jail terms for those who abuse Canada's immigration laws. Under existing legislation, for instance, the captain of the Amelie, the ship that arrived last year in Nova Scotia, could only be fined $5,000 and receive a maximum sentence of two years.
This is an insignificant penalty when 174 people are each prepared to pay several thousand dollars for an unauthorized voyage to Canada. When I spoke to the Senate committee in December, I addressed the issue that was most frequently
raised by the committee and its witnesses-the issue of Bill C-84's compliance with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
As 1 told the senators, during all of the months of the Government's consideration of solutions to abuse of the immigration program, Charter compliance was foremost in our minds. I rejected any suggestion that the Charter simply should not apply to persons who are not Canadian citizens or permanent residents of Canada. The Charter applies equally to all people regardless of their status in Canada. That is the law and Bill C-84 is consistent with the law. This view was affirmed by the expert counsel I have received from the Department of Justice.
As I also told the Senators, I do not want any person to be able to escape the operation of our laws because of a technical deficiency. I told the senators that I would be happy to consider any amendment that would give lawyers less to argue about-provided such an amendment does not weaken the operation of the Bill.
The Senate has now reported and I have reviewed the Message from the Senate carefully; there are 20 amendments, under 1 3 headings. Nine of the Senate's proposals are acceptable to the Government, at least in principle, but minor amendments to some of these proposals are necessary in order to ensure that the Bill will achieve its purposes, and to ensure that the amendments will fit the technical scheme of the Bill.
The amendments 1 am prepared to accept are these. One, to substitute the term «illegal entry® for the word «smuggling* in the Bill's statement of objectives. This will ensure consistency between the English and French text. Two, to amend the English version of Subsection 103.02(1), changing, for issuing a search warrant, from «evidence may be found® to «evidence will be found®. This amendment corrects a technical flaw in the English version of the Bill; to permit the judge to review the reasonableness of the security certificate. This change clarifies what had been intended from the outset, and makes it clear that the review will be made on the basis of all the information available. Three, to provide discretion to the Federal Court judge with regard to the persons of the person concerned at hearings involving alleged security risks. This is a change which emphasizes considerations of fundamental justice in a system of security review that is stronger than that which currently exists.
[ Translation]
To require the personal, written consent of the Attorney General of Canada or the Deputy Attorney General for the prosecution of those who organize illegal migration. This amendment adds further substance to the Government's undertaking that a person who violates the Act in the cause of rendering needed humanitarian assistance to refugees will not be prosecuted.
January 26, 1988

To provide for a weekly review of the detention of unidentified arrivals and suspected security risks by an adjudicator. This change maintains the additional powers for detention, but ensures compliance with the Canadian law that every person detained by the government has their detention reviewed by independent tribunal.
Other amendments which would alter the principles and objectives of Bill C-84,1 cannot accept.
First, security risks-right to claim. The Senate wants us to grant the right to make a refugee claim to persons who have committed a serious crime or who pose a risk to the security of Canada. It also wants us, Madam Speaker, to provide special detention review hearings for those held on ministerial certificates endorsed by the Solicitor General and myself.

This makes no sense whatsoever. No country has an obligation to protect a person who is a serious criminal or who constitutes a threat to its security. The Senate has already accepted this principle in the case of war criminals and, in any event, the 1951 Geneva Convention on refugees specifically excludes such persons from the benefits of the conventions. Even if we give such people access to the refugee board for a hearing on the merits of their claims-and even if they are found to be refugees-we are not obligated to let them stay in Canada. They should and will be removed whether or not they are refugees. The Senate proposals guarantee that such persons will claim, because they will be able to litigate against removal for months if not years, and the Canadian public will bear the risk and the expense. All this will do is ensure that those security risks who do not wish to leave will be able to retain a foothold in Canada. For this reason, Madam Speaker, I cannot accept the Senate's proposal.
Let me turn now to the matter of power to turn ships away. The Senate wants to rescind any power by which I could turn ships away. It is important to note that this provision provides the power to turn ships away. It does not stipulate that such measures must be used in all cases. It is very important to understand that this power must be retained to send a clear message world-wide that Canada will no longer tolerate abuse of our refugee determination system.
It is true that some genuine refugees must use boats to flee their country of origin and to find asylum in a neighboring country. The Vietnamese boat people provide an example with which everyone is familiar. That is not the kind of situation in which we would consider turning ships away. Our concern is with ships that bring illegal immigrants to Canada from safe countries, those which are signatories to the refugee convention and which have good records of compliance with their obligations toward refugees.
Let us remember that people who use ships to come to Canada illegally from safe countries are not fleeing for their lives. They are not escaping from oppression or inhumane
Immigration Act, 1976
conditions. They are simply seeking to improve their economic circumstances. They have all the characteristics of those who want to immigrate to Canada, but who are not willing to submit to the legal processes in order to do so.

It as been argued, Madam Speaker, that the most effective deterrent would be to bring the ship into port and to confiscate it. I cannot agree. Such a «half-measure* would still permit large numbers of persons to enter Canada illegally.
By retaining the power to turn ships around-even if that power is used only on rare occasions-we will be depriving the racketeers who promote such schemes of their main selling point: guaranteed entry to Canada.
By casting doubt on the success of these ventures, we will reduce the incentive for people to pay the high price which the racketeers demand, and we will diminish the appeal of such schemes.
For this reason, I cannot accept any changes to this provision. In order to provide yet another safeguard, however, I am proposing an amendment which will insure that the decision to use this power will be taken personally by the responsible Minister.
Because this amendment is not within the scope of the Senate's message to the House, I must seek unanimous consent from the House to incorporate it into my message to the Senate. I urge all Members to support this amendment.
I will also be seeking unanimous consent for an amendment that will make the definition of «exigent circumstances# more precise by substituting the word «means* for «includes* in Clause 11 of the Bill.
Other provisions which the Senate wants to change are equally important.
The Senate wants to limit prosecution for misrepresentation only in those cases where the claims are manifestly unfounded. I think this proposal is simply unworkable. We need to be able to curb misrepresentation as soon as it is detected. The restrictions proposed by the Senate mean that we would not be able to do so. Prosecution would only take place after the Government proves that a claim is unfounded, which may be weeks or months after the offence is detected.
The Senate also wants to limit the powers of search and seizure to daytime hours and to confine warrantless search to instances where lives are at risk. If we accept the amendment, we will seriously hamper the ability of our officers to apprehend and prosecute those who organize groups of illegal migrants. Transborder schemes would be conducted mainly at night so the perpetrators could escape Canadian jurisdiction if something went wrong.

January 26, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
This proposal means that in winter months when darkness comes early, the time of day during which effective action could be taken would be greatly reduced. What could we say about the North where sometimes there is one hour of daylight a day?
Finally, the Senate wants to restrict the penalties for organizing illegal migration to those events carried out in a clandestine manner. If we adopt this proposal, we would see ships steam right into Halifax next summer with unauthorized passengers and we would not have the power to do anything about it. The practices we are trying to deter are not always clandestine. We want to deter all forms of illegal entry. Therefore, we cannot accept this Senate amendment.
I have, however, accepted the Senate's proposal that all prosecutions under this provision should receive the consent in writing of the Attorney General of Canada. This measure, as stated earlier, adds further substance to the Government's undertaking that a person who violates the Act in the cause of rendering needed humanitarian assistance to refugees will not be prosecuted.
[ Translation]
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I will not accept any amendments to Bill C-84 that change the principles or objectives of the Bill. The amendments I am ready to accept will meet the basic concerns raised in the Senate's report.
I do not believe that we need to go further. Indeed, we cannot go further.

Canada's refugee determination system is strained to the breaking point. Bill C-84 aims to solve a clearly understood problem of abuse and to do so through the full application of the Charter. Parliament was recalled in August to deal with the urgent problem of a refugee determination system under siege. That urgency remains. We cannot permit further delay of our efforts to deal with it.
[ Translation]
I would therefore call upon the House to deal quickly with the motions that I am introducing. I urge this House to accept those amendments that are in accordance with our objectives and to reject those that would impair the effectiveness of Bill C-84.
Madam Speaker, I move the following amendments:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this House agrees with amendments 8 and 13(e) made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, but disagrees with amendments 4, 5(a), (b) and (c), 6(a) and
(b), 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13(a), because this House believes they contradict the principles of the Bill for the following reasons:
Amendment 4 would exclude only criminals and war criminals from the refugee determination process, but would allow terrorists, spies and subversives to pursue a claim to refugee status, notwithstanding the fact that Article 33 the UN Convention would permit the removal of these latter individuals to
their countries of nationality or permanent residence, even if they were determined to be Convention refugees.
Amendment 5(a) would eliminate the authority of the Minister to direct a ship to leave or not to enter Canadian waters. This amendment would reopen a significant gap in Canada's ability to control its borders.
Amendments 5(b) and (c) arise out of Senate amendment 5(a), which is not acceptable, and are therefore inappropriate.
Amendments 6(a) and (b) would reverse the policy on which the Immigration Act, 1976 was based, which policy was not changed in the Bill as passed by this House. The amendments jeopardize the possibility of successfully prosecuting persons who profit from organizing illegal migration and from counselling fraud among refugee claimants.
Amendments 9 and 10 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to act quickly to search for evidence of major offences under the Immigration Act, 1976, in exigent circumstances, where lives are at risk or where evidence with respect to those offences may be lost or destroyed.
Amendments 11 and 12 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to execute search warrants which have been duly authorized by a Justice of the Peace, by denying explicit autority to break open containers where it is reasonably believed evidence will be found and by limiting the authority to execute these warrants at night.
Amendment 13(a) would reduce the initial period of detention without review from seven days to forty-eight hours, which would allow insufficient time for the gathering of information to substantiate allegations or to identify the individual, particularly when large groups of undocumented persons arrive at one time.
