Madam Speaker, on behalf of the Liberal Party I am pleased to respond to the motion just put before the House of Commons by the Minister. I would like to begin my remarks with a commendation for the
Immigration Act, 1976
work done by the Senate. It should be noted that Liberal Members of the Senate have not moved amendments to the Bill in order to delay or as a tactic to frustrate the will of the House of Commons. Rather, this is a position adopted unanimously by all Senators on the Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs, including Conservative Members of the Senate. That speaks volumes about the kinds of amendments that have been moved. On this issue the Senators were not moved by any partisan feelings on Bill C-84, but were genuinely moved to improve a piece of legislation which was flawed seriously.
I would also like to congratulate the Senate for paying attention to the many deputations, representations, and witnesses which came before the Senate committee. There were many groups, individuals, and representations which were denied an opportunity for input because in the summer months the Government rushed the Bill through committee and through the House of Commons. At the very least the Senate deliberations provided a forum for those, particularly from the regions of the country, who were unable, on such short notice, to change their schedules, come to Ottawa, and make their views known.
I would like to pay special tribute to the Chairman of the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee, Senator Joan Neiman, who was a pivotal and very sensitive factor throughout the deliberations of the Senate. In short, democracy was well served by the report of the Senators in the other place.
There are a number of clauses in Bill C-84 which have no business being there. There have been a number of changes adopted by the Minister, although those changes are less of a priority when compared to some of the bigger ticket items which the Government refused to move on. However, it is still a sign that the Government was prepared to show more flexibility than it did during the summer months when this debate came to the fore with great passion and emotion.
There was a trickle of understanding and warmth which was completely absent during the debate in the summer. That recognition emanated since the summer debate and is a by-product of a Government which has reflected upon what it did. The Government has seen that the piece of legislation introduced in the House in the summer was overkill. It went far beyond the necessity to update legislation. When discussing this issue with Canadians last month they gave a different view than they did in the heat of the moment. I believe that Members, if not Ministers, of the Government have recognized that they went too far with that piece of legislation.
Therefore, even though the changes are few and of less priority than some of the other items in the legislation, there is still a recognition that the Government erred in its approach, in its contact, and in communicating to the Canadian public what we were dealing with. I believe the Government feels a certain amount of remorse for having fabricated that crisis, remorse

January 26, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
for having brought Parliament together. The Minister says that we are still in an urgent or emergency situation. Yet in discussions with the Senate committee and with the Senators we find there was absolutely no pressure, no signals from the Government of the day that it wanted that legislation quickly. There was no order from the Government to the Senators on that committee to rush through that committee as Bill C-84 was rushed through the legislative committee of the House of Commons. I believe that when the Government stepped back it began to realize that the crisis was a figment of its public relations imagination this past summer when its poll ratings were at 22 per cent at best. That was the impetus for the fabrication of the so-called crisis.
That brings into play the question of the role of Government if it is not to educate, to inform and to mobilize a progressive, understandable and calm public relation opinion towards very sensitive issues of the day, of which the immigration and refugee policy is an important part. Instead there is no leadership offered. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) talked about queue jumpers and illegal aliens. We had the situation in the last number of years where family immigration is down and entrepreneur immigration with the $250,000 capital investment is doubled. We are in a mess with respect to the backlog in refugee applications, and we have seen the spectacle of three or four high profile individuals who were clearly undesirable and who had come into this country notwithstanding. Therefore, we had a confusion of priorities, a lack of direction and a bankruptcy of leadership. That has bled the public confidence. That is really where the haemorrhaging is.
When we look at this piece of legislation, we must compare it with other issues. We must put into perspective the 330 individuals who came in by boat and asked for refugee asylum. I will admit that perhaps a few of those individuals, who knows, might not have been legitimate. A few might not have been true refugees, and a few perhaps should not have received the compassion of this country. Time will tell which of those individuals, if any, fall into that category. But we must compare the reaction of this Government to the reaction of the Government headed by the then Prime Minister, the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), in 1979, followed by the Government of Pierre Elliott Trudeau in 1980. What was their reaction when the world was asking its countries to come in and collectively help out with the Vietnamese boat refugee crisis? What was the reaction of our country then? We accepted over a two-year period, be it under the former Prime Minister, the Hon. Member for Yellowhead, or former Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau, 106,000 Vietnamese refugees. That was above and beyond every other aspect of the program. There were 50,000 sponsored by the two Governments, and the other 50,000 were sponsored by communities.
I ask you, Madam Speaker, was it not a challenge of the Governments of that day to educate the Canadian public as to why we should try to help out in this world crisis? Should we not have educated the public as to why communities should
open up their doors and their hearts to these individuals? These communities did that, and these are the same Canadians who live in our communities across the country today. These
106,000	refugees were allowed into the country with understanding and a sense of compassion and pride, and they are now integrated into Canadian society. They hold good jobs. Many of them own their own homes. Many of them have businesses, and their children, by and large, are doing extremely well. That is a successful and proud example of a people complemented by the best political leadership.
I ask myself where that leadership was when this Government was faced with a response to 300 people over two summers. The Senate began its deliberations and when it presented its recommendations, which represented the views of both the Conservative Party and the Liberal Party, I think the recommendations had two things in mind. The first was to try to maintain and keep the traditions that have made us a world leader in terms of assisting the plight of refugees. Therefore, the Senate wanted to instil some modifications in the Bill in order to try to have a piece of legislation which was moderate and in keeping with the progressive attitude that has shaped our policies over the long course.
1 recall the words of Rabbi Gunther Plaut who came before our committee during the summer and gave a very moving testimony before the committee. He said: «1 think the Bill was drawn in undue haste. This is why I think we need just a little more leisure to write legislation that makes sense®. He said: «1 think Draconian and emergency legislation gives the wrong signal not only to the world but to our own people in Canada®. He asked the members of the committee to look carefully at some of the amendments suggested. He said: «Do not follow the worst instincts of people, but follow their best instincts®. 1 think those words really provided guidance to members of the Senate committee who took those words to heart and made the changes that would allow that legislation to be in keeping with those traditions.
I believe the second impetus was to ensure that we would not be getting into any constitutional crisis vis-a-vis our Charter and laws. There was the fear that upon proclamation of this Bill into law, lawyers across this country would challenge this piece of legislation in the courts as a violation of certain aspects and sections of our Charter. What would happen then if one of those courts agreed with those arguments? It would cripple and paralyze the refugee policy yet once again. What would Canadians say then after being told by the Government that their concerns were taken care of? It would bleed confidence all the more. It would make the haemorrhaging problem even greater.
Therefore, we must recognize as parliamentarians that when adding up all the things we do, from constituency case files to speaking up on the floor of the House of Commons and in committee, we have two responsibilities that really dominate our work in this place. First, we must collect tax dollars and spend them wisely. Second, we must create and draw up good
January 26, 1988

legislation in keeping with our Constitution and Charter to govern Canadian citizens. I submit to you, Madam Speaker, with all due respect, that it is simply unacceptable for the Government to bring forward a Bill, in the full knowledge that there are serious legal and constitutional flaws in that piece of legislation. Rather than racing through this legislation only to be sorry later, the message from the Senate, and, indeed, the message we departed with in the summer, was to take care of those legal flaws now in order to avoid complications later on.
I would also like to take a moment to discuss some of the amendments and recommendations for changes that were not approved by the Minister in his statement only moments ago. He mentioned that he did not agree with some of the statements since they were against the principles of the Bill. I question what the principles of the Bill actually are in light of the fact that some of the recommendations made by the Senate are sensible and in keeping with the very premise and objective of the Bill.
The first recommendation he rejected was with respect to the clause put in by his Government that would enable a Minister or the Government to turn back a boat. In the summer we felt, and we feel now, as the Senators do, that this is the wrong clause to have in any legislation. It offers no due process to those people who may be on board a boat. The Minister talked about the fact that people on these boats are largely economic refugees. How does the Minister know this? How will he know how many are on board? How will he know who is on board? How will he know from where they are coming? How will he know what are their ages? How will he know what their health is on board the boat? The whole question of the unknown is a big variable that the Government simply cannot dismiss.
We cannot have the Minister woken up one morning by a call from his Deputy Minister saying to him, «Turn the boat back*. There is human cargo on these boats. Their cargo is not wheat or some raw material. They are not carrying shipments of steel. There are human beings on board who may in fact be legitimate refugees. We cannot afford to be flippant about this type of human cargo.
If the Minister is allowed to turn back a boat, then clearly the operative words become «mode of transportation®. If a relative of mine were to flee his country as a refugee and come by air to land at Pearson International then he would be processed once he said, «I am a refugee®. If another relative of mine from the other side of the world, who also may be a refugee, were to take a boat, that person would not receive the time of day. How can we allow the mode of transportation to dictate how the system will process such a person? Such a thing cannot be allowed. There is but one system and one law. There is but one category and one class of refugee. There are not two classes dependent upon whether one arrives by boat, plane, bus, or whether one arrives riding a bicycle across the border from Buffalo. The fact of the matter is that there should be
Immigration Act, 1976
one response by the system to a person, irrespective of how he or she come into the country.
The last aspect of this whole matter is the most curious. My contention is that turning back a boat does not discourage the manipulators or the traffickers of human flesh about whom the Minister spoke. According to his statements today he stated in his press release that some amendments, including turning back a boat, attempt to change the principles of the Bill, and that some do not support its over-all intent. He said therefore that he could not accept these amendments.
My question to the Minister is this. How will this turning back of a boat discourage smugglers and traffickers from trying the whole process again? As the legislation is written now the Minister can turn back a boat. He seems to think that that will discourage another boat from arriving. I ask Hon. Members to put themselves in the place of a smuggler, the captain of a boat. All he has to lose is the fact that he might be turned away. Thus there is a 50 per cent chance that he will dump his human cargo in Canada and a 50 per cent chance that he will be turned away.
If he is turned away, then perhaps he will dump his cargo a little further out, or else he will dump it on another part of the coastline, or even take his cargo to another country. The captain, the smuggler, does not care because he has received cash on delivery. By this point in time he has already pocketed the $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 fee. He really does not give a hoot as long as he has the dollars in his pocket. If there were a second captain about to leave from another port, would he be discouraged from leaving with a new shipment of refugees? I think not.
What does the Senate suggest? It articulated the recommendation that rather than turning back a boat it be escorted into port. If we want to punish these smugglers of human misery then we should bring the boat in, confiscate it and sell it, and punish the captain by imposing a fine upon him or by placing him in prison. If we were to do that with a boat which arrived today and the message went back to all ports that the captain had lost his boat and is in prison, do Hon. Members think that another captain would leave harbour risking imprisonment and losing his livelihood? I think not.
The discouragement is greater if we bring the boat in and then punish the culprits. We will also be more wise since we will be able to question the captains. We can even try to break down the rings and the networks that are operating throughout the world. How wise would we be just to turn back a boat? It would not discourage anyone. We would only find the next morning another boat in another harbour.
When the Minister says that these recommendations do not fulfil the principles of the Bill he is wrong. In part, one of the principles was to discourage human smugglers. Turning back a boat does not discourage human smugglers at all. What it does is to offer a public relations gimmick to the Government to try to communicate the message that somehow it is doing something about the so-called problem.

January 26, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Our suggestion is that the Government accept the recommendation to take in the boat and to punish those who need to be punished, allowing those who are on board the due process of law. We are not suggesting that, because someone is on a boat, that person is automatically a refugee. No one has suggested that, not the Senators, not myself, nor members of my Party. It will have to be established through due process whether or not these people deserve to stay in the country.
In this Bill the Government has created a new offence, a new fine and a new prison term for those who help refugees who might not have a valid visa. In addition to the question of turning back a boat, the recommendation in this regard probably summarizes the frustration that Canadians have with this piece of legislation. I would be embarrassed if my Party forced me as the Minister to put such measures in the legislation. What will be done through the implementation of such measures is to create civil disobedience for those such as priests, nuns, or the average layman who helps a refugee come into the country without the proper documentation.
Does the Government realize the impact of such a measure? Does it know the reality of the true refugee? I think that after a period of time in his position the Minister should know that sometimes the true refugees do not have the time to line up to obtain a visa document. Sometimes they have to forge such documents in order to get through the Customs of the country they are fleeing. Sometimes they do not even have the time to do that as they are being pursued. They simply get on the first plane or boat and get out of that country. Therefore they come to Canada without the proper documents that Members of Parliament, our families and other Canadians have six months to validate.
This measure puts the operative word on the document. It goes beyond that and states that if a priest were to help someone to come into the country who did not have a legitimate visa, he or she would face a possible fine or prison term. That runs counter to the life of the true refugee. It is offensive. It is offensive to those organizations and religious institutions that have made it a career and interest to help those refugees.
When one thinks about other issues, it has been the churches together with many organizations that have been at the forefront of the social issues. It has not been the Government, regardless of its stripe, but the churches that have attempted to feed the hungry and started the phenomenon of food banks in order to help. It is the churches and other organizations that have given shelter to the homeless. It is the churches and others who have helped the aged, the lonely, and the depressed. Now they are also helping those who do not have a country, not because of choice, but because of pressure, torture, assassinations, and threats.
They are now going to be punished if those individuals do not have the proper documentation. I find that offensive and
embarrassing, even as a member of the Opposition. It will go down in the history of Canada that it was this Parliament that passed such a regressive piece of legislation with such an offensive clause to make it civil disobedience if a priest or nun helps an individual come through without the proper visa.
We suggested wording changes. As did the Senate, we suggested that it should be illegal for any church or other member of Canadian society to counsel individuals on fraudulent claims, or to advise individuals on fraudulent applications, or to establish, forge, or write the wrong visa documents.
They told us before both committees of the House and of the Senate that they would accept that. They do not want to be above the law. I have heard the Minister of Immigration on numerous occasions suggesting that somehow they want to be above the law. They want to be within the law. But we want to create a law that is respectable and a reflection of Canada in 1987-88 and not some sense of a society as it was back in the days when anything went.
This clause should not be looked at in a flippant manner. Many of those organizations will in fact be breaking the law. They have told us so themselves. I recall the words of Nancy Pocock from the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees who stated:
If my Government tells me it is a crime to help these people. I will have to
say I am obeying a higher law and I am going to continue to help them when
they need me.
Therefore, there are citizens who have been forced to say that they are prepared to break the law. They are prepared to break the law not because they do not want to preserve a sense of order and fair play in this country, but because they do not respect the law. They do not respect the impetus behind the creation of this law, and they do not believe that it is just and fair and that it should be part of our system.
1 was taken aback that, on those two primary recommendations about escorting the ship into port as opposed to sending it back, and not to create a new offence for those aiding and abetting legitimately, the Government did not move on those two aspects to bring it into line with the Charter, with the Constitution, and with the premise of the Bill.
Another area of contention was the search and seizure. The Minister mentioned that he did not want simply to use a warrant during the day, he wanted it in the evenings. He suggested that the Senators were saying that once it hits four o'clock in the afternoon they are not allowed to get a warrant because it is part of the evening. The Senate said no such thing. The Senate was suggesting that it would be more in keeping with trying to get the warrants during the day. But if the situation merited it, if the ship was getting away and it was eight o'clock at night, there was nothing in their recommendations that stopped the Minister or the Government from executing such a search and seizure.
January 26, 1988

There too the clauses went far beyond the need and the necessity of this legislation. It was almost suggesting that they wished to make immigration officials into Rambo-like people rampaging the country, opening and breaking at their leisure. Is this the type of country that Canadians want? Are those the type of laws that we have developed and nurtured over the years? Of course, they are not. The laws and regulations that we as a society have nurtured have been far more moderate, tolerant, and intelligent than simply providing wide powers that one day may be abused by some Minister or Government, regardless of political stripe.
Therefore, we thought that some of the recommendations proposed by the Senate with respect to the search and seizure powers would be taken back somewhat. Not for one moment do we want to take away the tools of any Government to ensure the security of our country. There are tools presently in place to look after our country. After all, I think that we have been doing a pretty good job all these years. There must be something in place that has allowed us to protect our borders. The tools are there now. We should improve those tools, yes, changing with the times to meet the new challenges, but certainly not galloping ahead into regulations that leave open the serious possible abuse of rights of Canadians citizens and noncitizens alike.
Another similar aspect of the Bill was the detainment provisions. This summer Senators, including government Senators and Members of Parliament, pleaded for some moderation in terms of the tools that they wanted in place. The existing regulations provide that anyone can be detained for good reasons for up to 48 hours without any questions asked. In order to continue to detain the person following 48 hours, the law requests that the Government must get approval from an adjudicator. That approval will be granted for one week, at which time that approval needs to be re-established.
Therefore, if there are good grounds for detainment, for example, if the identity papers have not come in from some other country, or if there has been a delay or questions, the adjudicator will provide an extension. No adjudicator in this country will abandon the security considerations of Canada because it is also their country. Any adjudicator worth his or her salt will obviously have to balance the interests of the country from a security viewpoint and the variables of individual rights. He or she will weigh them.
But let us remove and depoliticize that decision-making. Let us have a politically disinterested person, that is, an adjudicator making the decision as opposed to a politically motivated individual, for example, a cabinet Minister or a deputy minister.
Our system would be far healthier if that were the course taken, rather than giving great powers vested in a Minister who can basically detain at whim, simply with a rubber stamp. The proceedings are that seven days would be automatically granted, following which a 21-day period must be granted if
Immigration Act, 1976
they so desire because there is no discretion offered to the adjudicator to change that.
The Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) is present in the House. During the lifetime of this debate in the House I ask him to reconsider perhaps the moderation aspect with respect to both search and seizure and detainment.
Another aspect was the whole question of security. To start with, it is a very sensitive issue. It is even more sensitive following on the experience with which the country has had to live in the last year in respect of the granting of immigrant status to a convicted terrorist. It is an extremely sensitive and emotional issue.
The Government suggested that anyone suspected of a security flaw should not have access to the refugee process or the refugee system. The Senate came back and said: «We believe that that should be the case for those who are convicted of a serious crime, for terrorism, and for convicted war criminals®. It indicated that those people should not have access to our refugee system to buy more time or to abuse the compassion of our country. I would agree with that. However, the Government wanted to go beyond that and talk about people it may suspect of some wrongdoing. Currently it wants to incorporate under Subsections 19(1 )(c), (e), (f), and (g) of the Immigration Act people suspected of undermining security or people suspected of having done so in the past. It is all based on suspicion. As the Prime Minister mentioned a number of times this week, we have in our system the presumption of innocence until proven guilty. Our point is that we cannot simply detain or order people out of the country based upon suspicions. It must be much more valid than that. We must also define what we mean by «subversive*.
Is Nelson Mandela a terrorist because he has tried to obtain freedom for himself and his people in South Africa? According to the definition, Nelson Mandela would be one of those individuals who would be seen to be undermining a Government of another land. He would be seen as going against the system. Currently Nelson Mandela is in prison and has been convicted of what South Africa thinks is a crime and what we would reward with a medal, namely, the seeking of one's democracy and freedom. Therefore we must try to define what constitutes subversive activities.
Our position has been that we need more than simply suspicion, and at the end of my remarks I will be moving an amendment which plays to that fact. On the one hand people convicted of serious crime have no business being in our country, let alone applying for refugee status. That is one extreme. The Government is going to the other extreme and saying: «Look, give us the power so that if we suspect somebody we can get rid of him rather than having them apply for refugee status®. That is the other extreme, and it is too much of an extreme because it can be abused. My amendment, which I will read into the record at the end of my speech, would do the following.

January 26, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
If the Government had a suspicion about someone in Canada undermining the security of our country or having done so and not having been convicted in another country, the Government would have to begin deportation proceedings and allow for due process. If the deportation proceedings were upheld, that is to say, if it can be proven that the suspicions are true, I would agree that thereafter the door could be closed and that they should not be given a second opportunity to buy more time for a second merry-go-round by saying: «I am a refugee®.
If the Government had suspicions about people who have not yet been convicted but are undermining security, we are mandating the Government to begin deportation proceedings immediately, which would trigger due process and a hearing. If the hearing concludes that they are a threat to Canadian security, following that judgment they should not be able to make a refugee claim. I think we are prepared to support that amendment.
We are also putting it forward in the spirit that I believe the country has learned something about our security system in the last two weeks about which I wish we did not have to learn. It is a balanced compromise which says that those who are convicted must leave the country and certainly have should not been allowed to apply for refugee status. Second, those who are suspected must have the due process of deportation proceedings, at the end of which they must leave or have their refugee application treated accordingly.
In conclusion, we wish to say that in part the objective is to curb abuse of the system. We have never said that everyone who has applied for refugee status is a legitimate refugee. We have never said that there has been no abuse. I wish we could have said that. We cannot afford to say that realistically about any aspect of Government. If we look at the unemployment insurance program we find abuse. If we look at the Canada Pension Plan disability provision, we find that there is abuse if people collect even though their backs or knees really do not hurt. We also know that there is abuse in terms of workers' compensation cases. Government tries to eliminate abuse without making disparaging remarks about the majority of cases which are legitimate ones. Therefore, if we have not turfed out the workers' compensation program, or the UIC program, or the CPP disability program, why should we turn the refugee program upside down because a number of individuals may have abused the system?
We are saying that no one should welcome, support, or reward those people who wish to abuse refugee procedures. At the same time we are asking the Government not to undermine what has taken many years to build up-a system of which Canadians are proud, a system which needs reform but, in the world context, is looked at with awe and envy in all corners of the globe.
During this debate we wish to submit a second conclusion to the Government. It should not get lost with the short term and
think that this is a temporary piece of legislation. It has a larger long-term perspective. The Government should be educating the Canadian public, not trying to undermine or decrease public confidence in the system. Immigration and refugee policy is a very important area which can help to make Canada a better, bigger, and more prosperous country. The Government should not ruin in the short term what is there for the long term.
It should also discuss with Canadians in a mature way the following facts. We have a dwindling birth rate, an aging population, 50,000 people leave the country every year, rates of immigration are higher in terms of targets than the actual number of people coming into the country, and we need individuals because our educational system is still not producing a sufficient number. For example, we still go to Great Britain to import tool and die-makers.
When we add together all these variables, we see that we cannot sacrifice educating Canadians on those needs. They can see the merits of immigration, that it has an important role to play in coming years. They know that Canada will continue to search, to promote, and to invite people to its shores to join in the building of the country, which never stops because we are always building and always have an eye to the future.
Let the Government not deny that future, that potential which is there for immigration to add to Canada, by inciting and fabricating a crisis which does not exist. Let us be more positive. Let us be more statesmanlike. Let us be more outward looking. That is our second message to the Government today.
[DOT] <1620)
Our third message is that policy is not only a domestic policy; but it is also a window to the world. It has international implications. We must recognize that as Canadians sometimes we do not promote ourselves or our policies as aggressively or as actively as we should, as Americans do, for example. We should recognize that here is an example of international diplomacy, a recognition of international leadership in trying to combat what is a world problem. This is not a problem only akin to Canada; this is a world-wide problem in need of a world-wide solution. Let us not again be followers as opposed to leaders. Let us continue to lead. Bill C-84 is not leadership. It is a message to the world that we are loosening the resolve of trying to combat this terrible problem of where people have to go when they are on the run. This is a message to Great Britain, to the United States and to Europe that they too can become lax. If Canada is being lax it must be right.
I ask you with all due respect, Madam Speaker, where is the international solution if all those countries take away what is there now? What will we have if we have that long corridor of internationally locked doors? Will it make the problem go away, or will it make the problem greater? Will it lessen the frustration of the refugees who see those locked doors, or will they become more desperate and will more of them run to underworld manipulators?
January 26, 1988

Therefore, the international message is rather than loosening the resolve, rather than softening the political international will, we should be putting out a strong message. If there was ever a time to strengthen that resolve, it is now. Canada cannot accept 10 to 15 million refugees. No one is saying that. It would be impossible physically and politically. We know that. The world together must solve the problem, but this type of legislation begins to undo that resolve.
Rather than creating Bill C-84s we should be calling for an international conference. We should be bringing together the Ministers of Immigration and the Foreign Affairs Ministers who should be looking each other in the eye and saying. «Are we still as resolved?* Does the Geneva Convention really mean a damn at the end of the road? Is the Geneva Convention simply becoming an empty piece of paper that is manipulated by every Government or opposition Party which points to the Geneva Convention? Everyone mentions the Geneva Convention in his or her argument to justify the argument. That to me makes it meaningless because it does not have a significant, realistic impact at the end. If we want to restore the Geneva Convention to its proper stature, we need that political resolve internationally. We cannot do it alone, and we know that. Canadians do know that. Canadians are proud of past Governments of whatever stripe which have had the courage and the conviction to stand up and be counted in trying to get an increasingly stubborn world dealing with this human dilemma before us all.
Those are the three messages we would like to deposit into the records of the House of Commons for the benefit of the Ministers and the Government to try to convince them that there are other recommendations, a major one in the Senate report, that will preserve our traditions, keep intact our leadership and promote the pride that Canadians feel about our policies. Reform the system, yes. Improve it, yes. Cut out abuse, yes. But devastate the policy, no. The message from Ottawa to the country and to the world must be an unequivocal, resounding no. We are staying our ground and leading the world in the right direction.
History is created by monumental decisions that we look back to. If Bill C-84 is allowed to stand as it is now, people will not look back to this Parliament in 30 or 50 years in any good way; just as we looked back to the Parliament which turned back a boatload of Jews many years ago. That action might have been popular then, but it is disgusting now. We have the ability to learn from our experience and to ensure that future Members of Parliament and Ministers will look back upon this legislation as a building block as opposed to a stumbling block.
Pursuant to my earlier discussion in moving an amendment to clarify the security aspect of the Senate amendments, I
Immigration Act, 1976
move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi):
That the message of the House of Commons to the Senate be amended by:
a)	deleting, in paragraph one, the reference to Senate amendment 4;
b)	deleting paragraph two;
c)	adding to paragraph nine a reference to Senate amendment 4; and
d)	adding after amendment 3 the following:
«That amendment 4 of the Senate be amended by deleting the said amendment and by striking out line 16 on page 7 of the Bill and substituting the following therefor:
«(2)(c) and against whom a deportation order has been upheld by the Board; or"*
With those words, Madam Speaker, I conclude my remarks and I look forward to discussing this amendment with the Government. I look forward to further changes and further flexibility exhibited thus far on some of the more minor amendments. We also need movement and change on the basic tenets of this legislation.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 M EASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, and the motion of Mr. Bouchard (p. 12300).

January 26, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976

I want to comment on the handling of the recommendations in this Bill. The first recommendation of the committee was to replace the word ((smuggling# with ((clandestine entry#. The Government claims to accept that in principle, but in fact it does not. By replacing it with ((illegal entry#, what they do in fact is to continue the same policy as was put forward by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to the legislative committee last summer in which he said that the phrase ((illegal entry# will mean that anybody who helps a refugee, a real refugee who lacks a visa, is committing a crime. In other words, the Government has not changed its policy by pretending to accept, with the weasel phrase «in principle#, the first amendment of the Senate.
The second amendment on security certificates, yes, the Government has accepted that amendment. That means that the Government will revert to the standard practice of justice in this country and let the court decide rather than some ministerial official, on the question of security certificates, that a person who is the subject of a security certificate should have the chance to be present during the presentation of the Government's case to the judge except where the judge, not the Minister, decides there are compelling reasons for exclusion. I am glad that the Government has accepted that amendment.
That was amendment 2(a). The second part of 2(a), however, the Government rejects. That really negates the value of the first amendment which they have accepted. That is, they will let the judge hear the case but they will not let him make a decision which he is qualified to make. They are saying that the amendment of the Senate would provide for a review of detention on the sole grounds of danger to the public. They say that that is too narrow and they will not let the court, the impartial court, override the decision of the Minister.
On Amendment no. 3, in the matter of security certificates, they have a rewording which may be adequate. They do not want to give us time to do a careful study of this. It may be that I will find, when I have had opportunity for further study on this during the next day or two, that there are problems there, but for the time being it looks adequate to say that this amendment would confirm that the judge is to assess the reasonableness of the certificate on the basis of all the evidence available to the judge.
Now we come to Amendment no. 4 which would allow people who are found to be security risks to make a refugee claim. Contrary to what the Minister and people on his side keep repeating, that is required of us by the treaty we signed 20 years ago with 100 other nations of the United Nations. Article 32 on expulsion reads as follows:
1.	The Contracting States shall not expel a refugee lawfully in their territory save on grounds of national security or public order.
Immigration Act, 1976
2.	The expulsion of such a refugee shall be only in pursuance of a decision reached in accordance with due process of law.
There is no due process of law there, Mr. Speaker.
Except where compelling reasons of national security otherwise require, the refugee shall be allowed to submit evidence to clear himself, and to appeal to and be represented for the purpose before competent authority or a person or persons specially designated by the competent authority.
Section 3 of Article 32 is the one where the Government fails in its international obligation by treaty. It says:
3.	The Contracting States shall allow such a refugee a reasonable period within which to seek legal admission into another country.
That is the reason for letting him make a refugee claim and have it decided whether or not he is a refugee, because if he is found to be a refugee he has a right under international law, by the treaty we have signed, to a reasonable time to find another country that will accept him. It goes on to say:
The Contracting States reserve the right to apply during that period such internal measures as they may deem necessary.
That could include detention if they are worried about what he might do while they are finding another country.
It is very ironic, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) a few weeks ago, when he was in Central America, suggested that Canada might take in some of the Contras. Some of the people who have killed, burned, and carried on war against the Government and the people of Nicaragua might be accepted as refugees in Canada, according to a statement by the Secretary of State. He later qualified the statement, but it is very interesting that it depends upon whose ox is gored. In other words, when he is in Central America as an ally of the United States he is willing to bend the rules and allow people in who should be excluded by this Bill.
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs ought to talk to his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and point out that Canada should amend this Bill as the Senate asked in order not to violate our international obligations under the United Nations Convention regarding the status of refugees which we signed 20 years ago.
We then come to the matter of turning the ships around. We find that even a good Tory newspaper, The Globe and Mail, agrees with the Senate and not with the Minister. In their editorial on January 5 they say:
Bill C-84 would, for instance, let the Minister turn ships away from Canadian waters if he thought they might be smuggling passengers-a response more dangerous to those passengers, and less intimidating to the captain, than seizing the ship and arresting the crew when the boat landed.
They go on to object, likewise, to further clauses of the Bill. They point out that what we should be doing is to bring the ship to shore, charge the captain with any offence that we believe he has committed, and deal with the passengers accordingly. That would have the effect of drying up the illegal traffic.

January 26, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
However, the principle of turning the ships away is part of Erik Nielsen's principle of hot flight only. In other words, the Government wishes to turn refugees away because they come from the wrong countries and they have the wrong colour of skin and perhaps the wrong politics. So the ship turning amendments, (a) and (b), have been rejected by the Minister and likewise amendment (c).
We now come to the infamous amendment on aiding and abetting. This says, in effect, that anybody who helps a refugee can be prosecuted for doing so if the refugee did not have a visa to enter Canada. Madam Speaker, it has been said time and again by everyone who knows about refugees that refugees most often cannot get visas, certainly not valid visas. This means to try to intimidate ordinary Canadians from doing what thousands of them have been doing and what thousands of them continue to do to this day, to intimidate them with the threat of a jail sentence.
The Minister claims that he has to do that, that he will not apply it to everybody but he has to do that to catch the guilty ones. In other words, the Minister is saying that our Department of Justice is so incompetent that it cannot define a crime. He has no confidence in the legal experts of our Department of Justice. There are 35,000 lawyers in the land who attack that clause through the Bar Association. 1 am sure they could easily provide the legal expertise, and I believe some of them would do it for free on a matter of conscience. The Minister is so contemptuous of the legal expertise of our Department of Justice that he says they cannot write a law that describes the illegal actions that violate our immigration security without attacking thousands of people whom he says he would not prosecute.
In Section 7 again the Minister weasels. He says he accepts in principle the amendment that would require the personal written consent of the Attorney General of Canada before a prosecution could be launched. That is what he actually proposed, so I understand, when he spoke to the Senate. But then, of course, he backed off from that and decided that that was not good enough, that it has to be the Attorney General and his deputy. He now has it that the Attorney General or the Deputy Attorney General can initiate the charge. In other words, he does not deal straight, even with his Conservative colleagues in the Senate.
Amendment no. 8 is accepted, and I am glad of that. They probably could not do any less since the Supreme Court, in the Hunter versus Southam case, made it quite clear that a search warrant should only be issued where there are reasonable grounds to believe that evidence will be found. In other words, the Government knows that it is prohibited from going on a fishing trip, from searching and seizing, in the hope that it might find some evidence. That is illegal and I am glad the Government has admitted it.
With regard to Amendment no. 9 on search and seizure, it is very interesting that in his message to the Senate the Minister misrepresents the nature of that amendment. That is very interesting, Madam Speaker. In speaking of Amendments nos. 9 and 10 he says they would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to act quickly to search for evidence of major offences under the Immigration Act in exigent circumstances where lives are at risk or where evidence with respect to those offences may be lost or destroyed. The amendment expressly says that where lives are at risk it may be done. They expressly allow for that, and the Minister has misrepresented them in order to justify his refusal.
I see you are signalling to me, Madam Speaker, that my time is nearly finished. I am very sorry that such a large subject as this is presented in such a hurry. I will have to rely on my colleagues to bring out some of the further faults. I wish merely to summarize by saying that this motion of the Minister must be rejected because it is contrary to our Charter of Rights as the Senate has explained in page after page of its explanations.
It is contrary to our treaty with the United Nations and a hundred other members of the United Nations with respect to the protection of refugees. It is a shameful and unacknowledged application of the policy of restricting refugees to people in «hot flight®, that is only from a very few countries, or to people chosen as immigrants for their economic value. Madam Speaker, I respect the work the Hon. Member has done and the many points he made during his address. However, I will not give a final opinion on his amendment for two reasons. First, it appears to me to violate Article 32 of the Convention, and this is a treaty that Canada has signed. It appears to violated the Convention because it would deny a person a chance to make a refugee claim. The United Nations is quite firm on that.
This is pioneering legislation on individual human rights. As a democratic socialist, 1 find it very illuminating that it is a Tory Government that attacks individual human rights internationally. This follows the Declaration on Human Rights by the United Nations in 1948, Article 13. It follows the Convention on the Status of Refugees of 1951, and the Protocol of 1967 signed by us in 1968. What that says is that a person has a right to seek asylum and protection from his own Government if it is persecuting him or allowing persecution. He has a right in law. We agreed with that law. Therefore, we should not deny it even though it is a little inconvenient or expensive.
We can keep him in detention if we are afraid of him or her, but we should not deny their right because it can make a difference to what happens after, and this brings me to my second point. He has to have a chance to choose another country, not necessarily to be sent back to, say, the Pinochet regime, which could declare him to be a terrorist or criminal on grounds that would not hold in Canada.

The matter was debated in the House of Commons, as it is being debated today as a Private Members' matter. At that point the Secretary of State indicated that if the Bill were withdrawn and the subject matter presented to a committee he would undertake to give government support to the measure and to produce an alternative Bill in the very near future.
In fact, he did that. In June of 1980, Bill C-36, which is the Bill that enacted the current National Anthem Act, was introduced and passed. As I have said, it is more than a historic note with respect to the procedure that took place in June of 1980 because that Bill was passed with the consent and concurrence of all the Parties in the House of Commons. However, it was on the particular understanding that the words provided for in Bill C-36 were not to be written in stone. Further changes were to be considered.
In fact, it was on the record of the House of Commons that it was anticipated that Private Members, through the medium of Private Members' Bills, would introduce changes in the House of Commons. Thus I want to use that to deal with this point. Some people say, «Do not change the national anthem. It is part of our history. It is changing our traditions*. That is not so. Anyone who knows the history of O Canada and the national anthem simply does not accept that as either factual or proper in theory or in terms of heritage. The O Canada was not adopted by the House of Commons until 1980. There was no official version until the National Anthem Act was passed in that year. It was clearly on the understanding that there would be changes from time to time, and particularly on the understanding that those changes would be brought to the House of Commons by way of a Private Members' Bill. We are exactly on course. There are changes in the National Anthem Act that I think are required with the evolution of our society. I believe they should be made. I believe the change removing the reference to «thy sons* is one of those changes that was contemplated when the National Anthem Act was adopted.
I wish to refer briefly to the constitutional process that has taken place in Canada over the last decade. I wish to remind Members that we all agreed to the Constitution Act of 1982. Some did not, some voted against it, but the great majority agreed with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In Section 28 it enacted the assurance that there would be equal rights for men and women, that there would be no discrimination based on sex.
I ask Members of the House of Commons how, on the one hand, they can see fit to enact Section 28 as part of our constitutional record, and reject the amendment that I proposed? It is not consistent. I have looked at the matter and I have come to that conclusion. I do not believe there is any justification for any other conclusion.
That brings me to my personal involvement with this issue. It was not a matter that I discovered. I did not go looking for
National Anthem Act
reasons to change the national anthem. I was approached by representatives of Mount Saint Vincent. It is an institution in the federal constituency of Halifax West that contains the mother house of the Sisters of Charity and a university of higher education dedicated to the interests of women. It accepts men as students, but everyone knows that Mount Saint Vincent University is the leading women's institution in Canada. It was suggested to me that this reference in O Canada was not consistent with our pattern of evolution in terms of equality rights for men and women. On examination I agreed that that statement was correct.
As a result, on June 14, 1984, I introduced Bill C-247 in the House of Commons, which is exactly the same as the Bill now before us. On the prorogation of that particular session 1 reintroduced the Bill in 1985, one year later. The whole matter has a history that did not start yesterday, but this is the opportunity to pursue and act upon the contents and substance of this Bill amending the National Anthem Act.
It is important that I cover the legislative process that might apply to Bill C-232 and its action before the House of Commons. As everybody knows, the motion is for second reading of the Bill and reference to a legislative committee.
Quite often when Private Members' measures gain acceptance in the House of Commons, the Member is asked to withdraw the Bill and consent to a reference of the subject matter to a standing committee of the House of Commons. I have had that happen in the past. It happened with respect to missing children's legislation that I introduced. It happened with respect to victims of crime legislation that I introduced by way of a Private Members' Bill.
That process is not appropriate to this Bill. I cannot help but think that anyone suggesting that the subject matter be referred to a standing committee of the House of Commons rather than reference of the Bill itself to a legislative committee, is really trying to assist in the process that would bring about this legislative change. I wish to tell you why, Madam Speaker.
Under the new rules standing committees that have an interest or jurisdiction over an area can deal with any matter they want. They do not need a reference from the House of Commons. If the committee responsible for the Secretary of State is interested in this change, it can go ahead and pursue it. It does not need a reference from the House of Commons.
I come here asking the House of Commons and my colleagues in this Chamber to refer this matter, this request for a change in the wording of our national anthem, O Canada, to a legislative committee. I do not think anything less than that reference to a legislative committee is acceptable. I do not think any Member will do any favour to the women of Canada who are interested in this issue, and all other persons who believe the issue should be acted upon, by suggesting any other course of action.

January 26, 1988
National Anthem Act
1 ask Members to take this matter in a serious vein, allow it today to go to the legislative committee. 1 am not wedded to the words that constitute the change. I simply believe that the change must be made. It is the only conclusion consistent with our endorsement of equality for the sexes. If we do any other action we will be called into ridicule by those interested outside.
We do not change the national anthem recklessly or without regard to the heritage of Canada and Canadians. We adopted the National Anthem Act in the House of Commons in 1980. We said it would be changed. That was part of the agreement by which it was enacted. Now it is time to give effect to those changes.
There may be other changes, but I present to the House one that I think is necessary and desirable. For those who would say, «Don't change it. Let it go. Do it another day. It is now part of our history#, I say that it is not yet part of our history. It will become part of our history, but it will only become an essential and honoured part of our history if we get the words right. Therefore, if we get the words right in 1988, O Canada will be sung for years, decades, and centuries to come by our sons and by our daughters with pride in the words and pride in the meaning. We will not be faced with these ludicrous distinctions.
I suggest to any Member of this House who wants to challenge me on this subject, who wants to pooh-pooh it, who says it is not necessary, it doesn't mean anything, my mother-in-law likes it, or my sister likes it that that is not the point. I say to Members and I say to everybody that, if you do not understand this point, if you do not take this point to heart, you do not understand equality.
I have found it to be the case, most unfortunately, that those people who denigrate a change like this are not in the forefront when it comes to equal pay for work of equal value. I find they are not there when it comes to positive action, employment opportunities for women, or any of those issues which are vital to the women of Canada. I do not want to suggest that this is an issue that is vital to the women of Canada, but it is a demonstration of the will of Parliament to give real meaning to equality, to give a meaning to equality, in this case to the sexes, but in another case to the equality of all Canadians.
Members of Parliament and colleagues in the House of Commons do not number yourself with those who stand against equality. Count yourself with those who stand for equality. Let this amendment go to the legislative committee, and we can all be proud of our national anthem.

Madam Speaker, I conclude with this question: What would our children and our descendants think if they came to realize that we were so pretentious and bold as to disguise our ancestral heritage in the hope of making it better?

For nearly four decades success at federal Governments have affirmed a commitment, both nationally and internationally to advancing the equality of women. But the issue here, I believe, is a recognition that our national anthem is part of our collective heritage, our identity as Canadians. This constituent wrote to the Hon. Member objecting to the phrase «native land* in the opening lines of our national anthem which reads: «0 Canada, our home and native land®. He objected because the word «native* refers to the land of a person's birth and excludes immigrants to Canada who cannot refer to Canada as their native land.
I believe this appeal, which was made on behalf of all immigrants who have chosen to come to Canada and have become Canadian citizens, is completely justified. I would like to point out that the The Oxford Dictionary defines the adjective «native* as meaning: «of one's birth, where one was born, belonging to one by right of birth or indigenous®. I think it is quite clear that when we are talking about our native land, we are referring to people who were born in Canada, not to people who chose to become Canadians but were born in other lands.

This second change in wording would, I think, be a significant gesture just as the Hon. Member's word change is to women. It would assure Canadians who were born in other lands that they indeed are first-class citizens in Canada and are not excluded from our national anthem or from anything else.

Madam Speaker, at the time of Confederation the country was preoccupied with the mechanics of unification and asserting a unique identity among the family members of world nations.
After Confederation Canada grew steadily, but in an orderly fashion. It was not until 1917, 50 years after Confederation, that we finally established our true independence in the eyes of the rest of the world. During that year, at the Battle of Vimy Ridge, Canadians served for the first time as a wholly Canadian force, emerging with distinction as victors. Other nations at that point came to regard us as an autonomous nation with our own strengths, Government and national character.
At that time the red ensign graced flagpoles around our nation, side by side with the Union Jack. As the years passed the Parliament and people of Canada expressed the desire that we have a new flag that would be readily identified as a symbol of Canada throughout the world. Some people today are sorry that there is not a bit of blue in that flag because it is my understanding that blue stands for integrity, white stands for peace, and red stands for sacrifice.
Adjournment Debate
Our own red and white banner of freedom and equality, with the distinctive Canadian maple leaf, was adopted by Parliament in 1964 and officially proclaimed on February 15, 1965, by the Queen. There are Members here today who were serving in Parliament at that time and I am certain each one of them remembers that day with fondness and pride.
Again, a fair amount of time passed before we obtained our own Constitution in 1982, but with the careful planning that went into that completely Canadian document we ended up with the finest and fairest declaration of self-identity in the world. We do things gradually, but we do get them right.
Madam Speaker, the story of our national anthem as well parallels such timely growth. Its inception dates back to 1880 when the French Canadian composer Calixa Lavallee wrote the music to a French text by Mr. Justice Routhier at the request of the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec. For a while English Canadians would still sing God Save the Queen or The Maple Leaf Forever.
In 1908 the Hon. Robert Stanley Weir penned the English version which, over the years, was given recognition by federal and provincial Governments for ceremonial occasions. Forty years later this became the official anthem of the Canadian Armed Forces by way of Order in Council.
Finally, in 1980, the 100th anniversary year of the music, our House of Commons adopted a Bill proclaiming O Canada as our legal, official national anthem. We have fondness for centennials in Canada, Madam Speaker.
These inspiring lines still make our hearts swell with pride when we see our flag wave, when our athletes excel in international competition, and when we travel to foreign lands and hear people speak with such respect for this nation we call home.

Madam Speaker, I rise in my place during this late show opportunity to raise a further question pursuant to a question I raised in the House of Commons on January 21. My question was directed to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) and concerned an incident to which Canadians have been treated for the last 10 days or so, namely, the incredible bungling of extreme proportions involving the convicted terrorist who was allowed to come into this country and then granted landed immigrant status.
As you know, Madam Speaker, from your knowledge of the regulations, such an individual would be clearly inadmissable according to our Act, yet not only did he find himself in this country but the Government actually approved his landed immigrant papers.
The Government was negligent in three areas; first, it did not find out about the true background of this individual in Spain from CSIS, which has the responsibility in our immigration proceedings, of making sure all applicants are security cleared. There are two essential tests with respect to individuals who want to come into this country. First there is a health check and, second, a security check. Enough resources are allocated to this area that cases such as this should be discovered.
The second mistake was that despite a telex alerting Pearson International Airport that this gentleman was arriving, this individual was able to walk right past immigration and Customs officials at the airport in Toronto without any questions being asked. That was the second time he got past our officials.
The third mistake, in our submission, would be that he was allowed to live in a Canadian community without any questions asked. He is a convicted terrorist who, in the words of the Government, did not pose a security threat, something I find somewhat odd given the individual's background.
Another question we raised is what happened in Spain? At what point did the Government commit this serious error. The Government and its Ministers have been defending the situation, saying it was the individual who misled Canadian authorities and it was on those grounds he was approved. We asked the question that was raised by the Toronto Star which suggested in its January 20th edition that the American intelligence service and the Israeli secret service had advised our Canadian officials in Spain about the individual's true identity and about his terrorist record. Despite those warnings, it is alleged by the Toronto Star that those officials somehow, for some reason, still saw fit to give this individual a security approval.
Our question was very specific. At any time did the secret service or officials from the Israelis ever make representations to Canadian officials? We asked the Minister to confirm or deny. He chose to do neither, which I think is significant
because if it clearly was a situation where there was no recommendation by these other two security forces, 1 think, politically and logically, the Minister would have taken the opportunity to deny the story. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary who will be responding tonight will inform us as to whether or not Canadian officials were advised and, in fact, requested by the other two security forces to not allow this person to get on board the plane. The Toronto Star states, according to its sources, that the officials knew of these recommendations even before the person boarded the plane.
The second part of the question was, if we give the benefit of the doubt to the Minister that the officials were misled, or ignored the individual's background, on what immigration criteria was this person allowed to come into the country? There are 12 factors including job, education, language, training, family, age, dependants and a number of other issues, which criteria must be met by all prospective immigrants.
Therefore, when one looks at this individual's unemployment situation in Canada, the fact that he is involved in a Manpower training program, and the fact that there are literally thousands of applicants with impeccable qualifications who get turned down every year with the story that they were misled, surely there must be some criteria by which this person was able to come into the country. We would like to know from the Parliamentary Secretary what that criteria was.
I look forward to the answer of the Parliamentary Secretary to both these very important questions.

After that time they received calls from a drug company, which had been given the information, offering to sell medication to both individuals. This matter was raised with the Minister. Those procedures are laid out very carefully.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, do you get home to your riding every weekend? I suspect that you try to get home. I certainly try to get home to my riding every weekend. January 26, 1988

I am sure you, Madam Speaker, receive a lot of mail. 1 receive a lot of mail at my constituency office, and I receive a lot here in Ottawa, but the mail I receive at home is of a certain variety. I suspect you know what I am referring to, Madam Speaker, that is bills! I suspect as well, Madam Speaker, that you may get a few bills in the mail, and you may have to write out some cheques when you get home to your constituency every weekend. I have that problem.
Last weekend when I went home and started opening my mail I found in those bills my real estate property tax bill for the first half of 1988. Not a very pleasant thought when I looked at the size of that bill and realized how that had escalated over the year. It disturbed me somewhat. In fact, it disturbed me a great deal. When I receive my property tax bill and look at it and think of what I am paying for in that bill, I think of policing. I am paying for the local police force. I think of the fire department. I am paying for the fire department. I am also paying for the garbage to be collected. I think of the local roads and sewers, and perhaps some of the recreation facilities and activities. These are the sorts of things for which I expect to be paying in my local property tax bill. I do not expect to pay for the cost of processing welfare payments to refugee claimants.
I do not know about you, Madam Speaker, but to me that seems to be something which really does not belong in the property tax. It does not seem as if when I pay my local taxes to the municipalities that I should have to pay for the cost of processing welfare payments to refugee claimants. It seems to me that some other level of Government should have that responsibility and, to my mind, it is the federal Government.
Before you say, Madam Speaker, that it is impossible that I should be paying for the processing of these welfare payments, let me tell you that the Metropolitan Toronto Community Services Department conducted a study on welfare claimants, in particular refugee claimants, back in July of 1987. It examined refugee claimants who were receiving welfare and found, in the month of July, that there were some 3,310 active cases of refugee claimants receiving welfare payments in Metropolitan Toronto. Just reflect on that number for a minute or two, Madam Speaker; 3,310 is the size of a good many communities and towns across the country.
Included in the costs of processing the payments for these cases were things like salaries and fringe benefits for employees, office space rental, and all that sort of thing. These 3,310 cases amounted in one month to $252,000 for the processing cost alone. I am not referring to the payments to the recipients, but just to the administrative costs of processing them-$252,000 for one month. That is over a quarter of a million dollars for one month and amounts to $3 million in one year.
As you may know, Madam Speaker, in the Province of Ontario the administrative costs of processing welfare payments are divided 50-50. The province and the federal Government pay 50 per cent of the cost and the local taxpayer pays the other 50 per cent. In this case the 50 per cent of the cost paid by local taxpayers through their property taxes for refugee claimants amounts to $1.5 million per year.
I want to stress that I am not talking about actual welfare payments to refugees, because there is some confusion in the department's mind on that, but I am talking about processing costs. The payments themselves are very substantially over that and are paid 100 per cent in the first year by the province and the federal Government. When we get to the processing costs, in fact only 50 per cent is paid by the province and the federal Government. I do not think that is a fair way of handling the processing of welfare payments to refugee claimants who are not, after all, the responsibility of municipalities but really fall within the jurisdiction and responsibility of the federal Government.
I do not know about you, Madam Speaker, but if you had to pay in Saint-Hyacinthe the processing costs of welfare payments for 3,300 refugee claimants, would you in fact think that it was fair? No, sirree, Madam Speaker, you would not think that that was fair. No, sirree, the Parliamentary Secretary who has a big smile on his face over there would not think it was fair if that were going on in Surrey, White Rock, or wherever.
I am expecting tonight that the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that the federal Government will live up to its responsibilities in respect of refugees and ensure us that it will cover all the processing costs for the administration of welfare payments to refugee claimants and that it will relieve me and other property taxpayers of having to pay these costs through our real estate taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I want to say that while all Members in the House have the right and the responsibility to raise questions that cover subjects of concern to them, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) has earned the right over and above the normal rights that we have in that he comes from local government activity and therefore understands how federal activities can impinge on local governments. He has also consistently in the House asked questions about subjects such as this one. While every Member has the right to ask questions which they may choose, the Member from York East has displayed a pattern about showing concern for fiscal responsibility, particularly as those burdens could shift to the local Government if the other two levels of Government do not do their share of the work or carry their fair share.
I have noted the Hon. Member's question. Unfortunately the question focuses more intently on the $1.5 million cost sharing program between the federal and provincial Governments. It is easy to lose sight in the question that there is also the ingredient of the cost of processing that $1.5 million. The Member stated that Metropolitan Toronto had asked the federal Government to pay at least a portion of the $1.5 million. I understand that the issue of refugee claimants and their impact on municipal services in Metropolitan Toronto was first brought to the attention of the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) last June. A report prepared by the Commissioner of Community Services called for a tri-level government committee to deal with the influx of refugee claimants. This resolution was supported by the Minister of State for Immigration.
January 26, 1988

The Minister wrote to the clerk of the municipality of Metro Toronto offering the services of Canada Employment and immigration officials in the Ontario region and welcoming the establishment of an intergovernmental committee to co-ordinate the planning of services to newcomers in Toronto. I understand that an introductory meeting has taken place which has set out parameters for the mandate of the committee and to establish membership.
As the Hon. Member is aware, the Canada Assistance Plan requires that provinces and the federal Government share the cost of income assistance on a 50-50 basis. As the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) pointed out in his reply to the Hon. Member's question, agreements between the provincial level and the municipal level are decided by these two parties. Having paid its 50 per cent of the cost, the federal Government does not interfere in the provincial-municipal cost sharing arrangements.
Might 1 add, and 1 think the Member understands this, that if the other place will do its duty to Canadians and make
Adjournment Debate
certain that it accepts the motion put forward by the Minister of Immigration today on Bill C-84 and passes Bill C-55 speedily, most of the questions which the Hon. Member has raised regarding this subject could be solved. The refugee claimants could then move from positions of being claimants to being landed immigrants or being asked to leave the country. That would relieve the burden from cities like Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal and would resolve from those refugee claimants what is at present a life of tension for them. If the Senate would do its job, we could get the job done.
